summary: A superconducting transmon qubit coupled to two transmission lines with asymmetric couplings ($\gamma_a = 100 \gamma_b$, $\gamma_a = 2\pi \times 72$ kHz) transfers power between them when driven by two spatially separated modes with canceling classical amplitudes, with the power flow direction controlled by the phase $\phi$ of the qubit's coherent superposition rather than classical parameters. The stimulated emission power varies as $\cos\phi$, reversing direction between $\phi=0$ and $\phi=\pi$, achieving a routing efficiency of 63% for an equal superposition ($|g\rangle + e^{i\phi}|e\rangle$ with $\theta=\pi/2$), close to the theoretical bound of 69% set by measured coherence times ($T_1 = 2.22$ µs, $T_2 = 3.21$ µs).
motivation: Understanding energy transfer between quantum systems and their environment through genuinely quantum parameters (coherence) rather than classical control knobs relates to quantum thermodynamics and waveguide QED, extending prior demonstrations of photon routing that relied on engineered classical phases or quantum state preparation as which-state bits.
method: A transmon qubit at $\omega_q/2\pi = 7.088$ GHz is driven by two transmission lines with opposite drive amplitudes ($\Omega_a = -\Omega_b = 2\pi \times 0.41$ MHz) so their net effect cancels ($H=0$), causing the qubit to undergo pure relaxation while continuously pumping power; output power in line a is measured via heterodyne detection after quantum-limited Josephson parametric amplification, and the Purcell rate is extracted from the transition between spontaneous and stimulated emission regimes by sweeping drive amplitude.
result: Time-resolved power measurements show the transfer amplitude $\delta\langle a_\mathrm{out}^\dagger a_\mathrm{out}\rangle \propto \cos\phi$, with maximum efficiency $\eta_\mathrm{max} = 63\%$ at $\langle a_\mathrm{in}^\dagger a_\mathrm{in}\rangle = 0.092$ photons/µs ($6 \times 10^{-2}$ photons total), and 46% efficiency for one input photon on average after $\tau = 2.7$ µs, compared to ideal limits of 69% and 54% from measured $T_1$ and $T_2$.
